title: Conjunctive Query Evaluation and Static Analysis
lead: Evaluating a query on one database is different from proving that two queries are equivalent on every database.
goals: Distinguish data complexity from combined complexity
Use the correct homomorphism direction when checking containment
Remove redundant atoms while preserving the output variables

sections.title: Two ways to measure difficulty
sections.html:
A database may have millions of rows, but a query can also become complicated. Which growth are we measuring? Keep Q(x) :- Buy(x,p), Premium(p) fixed while adding shoppers and products. Only the data changes. Now allow a user to submit patterns with any number of atoms and variables. Both the pattern and the data change. These are different computational problems.

We will ask a precise YES/NO question: given D, Q and candidate tuple a, is a ∈ Q(D)? This is membership. For the shopper query, ask whether An is in the answer. We need one premium purchase by An, rather than a printed list of every shopper. Printing a huge result already takes time proportional to its size, so it should not be confused with this decision problem.

Data complexity treats Q as fixed and measures growth in D. Combined complexity allows Q and D to grow. If a fixed query has k variables and n candidate values, exhaustive search tries at most nk assignments, with a fixed number of atom checks per assignment. A fixed k gives a polynomial in data size. This does not say exhaustive search is the best implementation.

When k is part of the input, that exponent is no longer a constant. General CQ membership is NP-complete in combined complexity, while it is in polynomial time for data complexity. “NP” says a YES answer has a certificate checkable in polynomial time; “NP-complete” also needs a hardness argument. Neither statement means every CQ runs slowly or that checking one proposed match requires searching all matches.

Try it: an application always asks the same three-atom query on a growing database. Which measure fits?

Data complexity. The query's variables and atoms remain fixed. If a query builder can generate an arbitrarily longer pattern, combined complexity becomes relevant. Always state what is allowed to grow before interpreting a bound.

sections.title: Worked example: count assignments and verify a witness
sections.html:
With three variables x,y,z and 100 possible values each, the assignment search has 100×100×100=1,000,000 possibilities. With 200 values it has 200³=8,000,000. With ten variables and 100 values it has 100¹⁰ possibilities. This explains the danger of growing patterns, but an expensive brute-force algorithm alone is not a proof that no better algorithm exists.

To verify a proposed YES answer for An in Q(x) :- Buy(x,p), Premium(p), receive the certificate x=An,p=pen. Check Buy(An,pen), check Premium(pen), then check that the head x equals An. If all pass, the certificate works. These checks are polynomial in the input; trying every possible p is not part of verifying this certificate. That establishes membership in NP.

Why the general problem is hard

Use a separate original graph-coloring example. Adjacent vertices must have different colors chosen from red, green and blue. Store the six ordered unequal color pairs:

Diff={(red,green),(red,blue),(green,red),
      (green,blue),(blue,red),(blue,green)}

A triangle becomes Q() :- Diff(u,v), Diff(v,w), Diff(w,u). Assignment u=red,v=green,w=blue passes all three atoms. Assignment u=red,v=red fails immediately because Diff(red,red) is absent.

For any graph, create one variable per vertex and a Diff atom per edge. A valid coloring supplies a match; a match supplies a valid coloring, since equal colors never occur in Diff. Construction size grows only with vertices and edges. Thus a general polynomial CQ-membership algorithm would solve the NP-complete 3-coloring problem in polynomial time. This reduction proves NP-hardness. Together with certificate verification, it proves NP-completeness.

Try it: add a fourth vertex adjacent to all three vertices of the triangle.

The triangle needs three different colors. The fourth vertex must differ from all three, but no fourth color exists, so no assignment matches. The database Diff stays the same; the graph's growth is encoded by adding variables and atoms to Q.

Key takeaway

The expression nk describes an algorithm; it does not prove NP-completeness. An expensive brute-force search does not rule out a better algorithm. Proving NP-completeness requires both membership in NP and NP-hardness.

sections.title: Containment: check the direction of the mapping
sections.html:
Can an optimizer replace a query without changing its answer? Testing a few datasets is useful but cannot prove equality on every database. Begin with two queries:

Qsmall(x) :- Buy(x,p), Premium(p)
Qall(x)   :- Buy(x,p)

Every match of Qsmall contains a Buy fact. Keep that same x,p and ignore the Premium test: it is also a match of Qall. Therefore Qsmall ⊆ Qall, meaning containment holds on every database. The additional requirement can remove shoppers, but cannot invent one who bought nothing.

To express this proof as a mapping, start with Qall's body and find its Buy atom inside Qsmall. Map x↦x,p↦p, preserving the output x. The homomorphism goes Qall→Qsmall, opposite to the containment arrow. Why? We locate the weaker query's requirements inside the stronger query so every stronger match can satisfy them.

Generally, Q1⊆Q2 exactly when a homomorphism Q2→Q1 preserves constants and the head tuple position by position. This theorem is for positive CQs with set semantics and without extra database constraints. A body-only match with a wrong head is insufficient.

The reverse containment fails on D={Buy(An,pen)} with no Premium facts. Qall returns An; Qsmall is empty. One counterexample disproves a universal claim. To prove equivalence, we need both containments, not merely two queries returning the same answer today.

Try it: compare A(x) :- R(x,y),R(x,z) with B(x) :- R(x,y).

B maps into A by identity. A maps into B by x↦x,y↦y,z↦y: distinct variables may share a value. Thus both containments hold and A≡B under sets. If the heads are A(x,y,z) and B(x,y), their different arities prevent this equivalence claim; a mapping must respect output positions too.

Key takeaway

The homomorphism arrow points in the opposite direction to containment. To show that every result of Q1 also satisfies Q2, find all the conditions of Q2 inside Q1.

sections.title: Canonical databases explain the proof
sections.html:
How can a finite mapping settle a claim about infinitely many possible databases? Construct a database that makes the first query's own requirements visible. For Qsmall, replace x and p by distinct fresh values cx and cp, keeping any original constants unchanged:

Dsmall={Buy(cx,cp), Premium(cp)}
Qsmall(Dsmall)={cx}
Qall(Dsmall)={cx}

This is Qsmall's canonical database. Qsmall has an answer by construction. Qall can produce the same head tuple using Buy(cx,cp). Renaming cx,cp back to the original variables reveals exactly the map Qall→Qsmall.

Try the reverse construction:

Dall={Buy(cx,cp)}
Qall(Dall)={cx}
Qsmall(Dall)={}

The missing Premium fact makes Dall a counterexample to Qall⊆Qsmall. More generally, construct D[Q1] using one fresh value per variable. If Q2 returns Q1's constructed head tuple, that match yields the head-preserving map Q2→Q1. If it cannot, D[Q1] itself disproves containment. The homomorphism theorem explains why this particular test is sufficient, unlike an arbitrary sample database.

A pure positive CQ is satisfiable because its canonical database witnesses its body. This conclusion assumes no extra constraints, inequalities or contradictory comparisons. It does not claim that the CQ has an answer on every existing database.

For unrestricted CQs supplied as input, containment and equivalence are NP-complete. Proposed mappings are polynomially checkable certificates; discovering them can be difficult. Equivalence needs certificates for both directions. These results do not automatically extend to SQL bags or NULL.

Try it: does an empty answer on your current database prove a pure CQ unsatisfiable?

No. Unsatisfiable means no database can supply an answer. The canonical database supplies one for this positive-CQ model. An empty current result may simply mean the required facts are currently absent.

sections.title: Minimization through a worked example
sections.html:
Removing repeated work is attractive, but deleting a condition can admit new answers. Start with Q(x) :- R(x,y), R(x,z), S(x). The two R conditions merely require some R partner for x; neither says y and z differ. If one R(x,y) exists, use z=y to satisfy the other. Hence Q(x) :- R(x,y), S(x) is equivalent.

Make the deletion argument explicit. The shorter body's atoms already occur in the original, so every original match satisfies the shorter query. For the other direction, extend every shorter match by setting z=y. Both directions preserve the head x.

Can we also remove S(x)? On D={R(a,b)} the proposed shorter query returns a, while the original has no S(a) and returns nothing. The deletion fails. Adding y≠z would also invalidate the earlier R deletion, and it moves beyond pure CQs. Changing the head to Q(x,y,z) prevents simply dropping the only binding for z.

Repeat the argument after each successful deletion

0: Q(x) :- R(x,y), R(x,'a'), S(x), S(x)
1: Q(x) :- R(x,y), R(x,'a'), S(x)
2: Q(x) :- R(x,'a'), S(x)

From 0 to 1, remove one identical S(x) check. From 1 to 2, use the fixed value 'a' as y: the remaining R(x,'a') also witnesses R(x,y). Neither step changes the head x or the meaning of a constant.

The quoted 'a' is a constant, not a variable. The final two-atom query has no equivalent proper subquery: dropping S admits {R(b,'a')}, and dropping R admits {S(b)}. Each database gives b after deletion but not before.

Such an irreducible equivalent CQ is a core. Cores are unique up to isomorphism, a reversible renaming preserving the head, atoms and constants. This structural uniqueness is not a promise of a cheap minimization algorithm. Check equivalence after each proposed deletion instead of counting atoms or trusting a convenient example.

Try it: may R(x,'a') be replaced by R(x,y) in the final core?

No. D={R(b,'c'),S(b)} with 'c' different from 'a' satisfies the replacement but not the original. Constants impose real requirements; renaming variables cannot erase them.

Key takeaway

Remove an atom only when the result is preserved on every database. Different variable names may use the same value. However, a variable in the head or an inequality condition can make a proposed simplification invalid.

quiz.question: To prove Q1 ⊆ Q2 using the homomorphism theorem, which mapping should you seek?
options: Only compare the number of atoms
quiz.explanation: The mapping goes against the direction of containment and must preserve the head and the constants.

source.summary: Lecture 24 studies the complexity of conjunctive-query evaluation, canonical databases, satisfiability, containment and equivalence through homomorphisms, and minimization to a core.

limitations: These theoretical results apply to conjunctive queries under set semantics. They do not automatically apply to SQL bags, NULL values, or additional constraints.
